newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vienna Philharmonic will have to admit women.
newsitem.headline: Vienna Philharmonic will have to admit women.

text.p: The Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra, one of Austria's last male bastions, will soon have to contend with women in its ranks at the prestigious state opera, the opera director told Reuters on Wednesday.
"I decided in mid January to (propose) admitting women with immediate effect," Ioan Holender said.
"I made the decision because I find it important and necessary. There is a law on equal treatment in Austria and the opera is a state institution."
The Vienna Philharmonic, founded in 1842 and famous for its annual New Year's concert, is a private association and its members play at the publicly-funded Vienna State Opera.

Holender said he had no say in the constitution of the Vienna Philharmonic, but predicted the staunchly male stronghold would not be able to withstand the widespread pressure to modernise and let in women for much longer.
Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima at a recent prize-giving ceremony urged the Philharmonic to "use the creative potential of the other half of mankind".
Helene Partik-Pable, a Freedom Party member of parliament, condemned the orchestra's stance on women as humiliating and said it should be forced by the government to employ women.
"If it is about maintaining the quality of the orchestra that is a flimsy excuse as women are more than capable of keeping up the standard through their equal skills," she said.
Asked if women could become a regular feature at the state opera, Holender said: "If they are good enough."
"In musical and artistic suitability, I don't see any reason why women should not play in the orchestra," he added.
So far just two female harpists have managed to break the mould at the opera, but it will take a long time for women to be represented equally in the traditional orchestra.
Even the privilege of standing in for a regular player is hard won. Substitutes, often students of Philharmonic members, must prove an outstanding skill to be nominated by orchestra musicians.
Opera musicians will hold a formal vote on the admission of women on February 27, just before the Vienna Philharmonic leave for a United States tour.
The all-male orchestra can expect vehement demonstrations and boycotts from U.S. feminist groups, according to international media speculation.
However, the Vienna Philharmonic is under no obligation to vote on admitting women.
Even if opera musicians vote in favour, according to convoluted rules members must wait three years before they can even apply for entry into the exclusive men's club.
